title: A comprehensive AI policy education framework for university teaching and learning
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapid rise of text-generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in higher education and the need for an institutional policy response. The author argues that universities need guidance on academic integrity, privacy, accountability, equity, and pedagogy because generative AI can both support learning and create risks such as cheating, over-reliance, reduced critical thinking, and unclear attribution of AI-assisted work.

The study uses a mixed-methods survey of stakeholders in Hong Kong universities. Data were collected from 457 students and 180 teachers and staff across disciplines through an online questionnaire with closed- and open-ended items. The quantitative component measured experiences and perceptions of generative AI use, while thematic analysis of open-ended responses identified key concerns and policy priorities.

Based on the findings, the paper proposes an AI Ecological Education Policy Framework with three dimensions: Pedagogical, Governance, and Operational. The framework emphasizes responsible use, AI literacy training, transparent governance, equitable access, monitoring and evaluation, assessment redesign, and support for student holistic competencies. The main conclusion is that generative AI should be integrated as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for human teaching, with policy structures to mitigate risks and maximize educational benefits.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based generative AI chatbot/system used for text generation and conversational assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper examines perceptions, risks, and policy implications of using ChatGPT and similar generative AI technologies in university teaching and learning.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods survey of 457 students and 180 teachers/staff in Hong Kong universities, respondents broadly supported institutional planning for generative AI (students mean=4.5, teachers mean=4.54 on the need for a plan to manage risks). At the same time, they expressed concerns about academic misconduct, unequal advantage in assignments, over-reliance, privacy, transparency, accountability, and weakened critical thinking and transferable skills.
findings.measure: Survey ratings and open-ended responses on perceptions of ChatGPT/generative AI, including risk management, academic misconduct, privacy/security, over-reliance, and effects on skills

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative and quantitative mixed-methods survey study, not an experimental evaluation of outcomes. It provides useful stakeholder perceptions and policy implications, but no causal estimate of tool effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial perceived impact on academic integrity, governance, and student skills, but these are attitudes and concerns rather than measured learning effects. No effect size is reported.
